# Bringing the encoders up to the decoders' speed

## Purpose

Since 1.2.0 the decoders became 1.5 to 9 times faster and the encoders did not move. Measured in one process on 2026-10-02, a Standard QR encode now takes about 2 to 5 times as long as decoding the same symbol (809 against 252 ns at version 1, 71.9 against 15.7 µs at version 40-L), while Micro QR and rMQR encode at about their decode speed. This plan makes the Standard QR encoder faster where its time goes, and trims the few fixed costs the other two share. The output does not change: every symbol stays byte-identical.

The measurements, how they were taken and a prototype are in [references/encode-performance-measurements.md](references/encode-performance-measurements.md). In short:

- Mask selection is 55 to 83 % of a Standard QR encode. Without it a version 40 encode would take about 13 µs, less than its decode.
- Two small changes (an index for the ECC table, shared finder-window terms in the AVX2 scorers) took the encode to 0.64 to 0.97 of its time with identical output.
- Skipping the zeroing of stack buffers with `[SkipLocalsInit]` gained 1 to 12 % at versions 1 to 10 and nothing measurable on larger symbols. It is not used: see What has to stay true.
- A scorer that also holds the matrix transposed, so that no penalty rule shifts bits across words, ran mask selection at 0.35 to 0.41 of the current time for versions 20 to 40 as an untuned prototype.
- The Alphanumeric and Numeric writers of `standardqr-binary-encoder-plan.md` are 3.2 to 9.3 % of an encode. That plan was set to run after the scorer work, when its share is larger, and ran as phase 7.

The README's benchmark images still show 1.2.0's numbers, and the repository's encode benchmarks time a matrix with a quiet zone while the decode benchmarks read one without, so the published encode and decode rows do not compare like with like.

## Scope

| In | Out |
|---|---|
| Standard QR mask selection: shared finder-window terms in every scorer tier, and a transposed scorer for versions 12 to 40 | Choosing masks differently (fewer candidates, another penalty, early acceptance). The chosen pattern is part of the output |
| Fixed costs on the Standard QR encode path: the ECC table lookup, the size of the hot methods' stack buffers, the forced mask path (F23 of the [2.0.0 plan](featherqr-2.0.0-plan.md)) | `[SkipLocalsInit]` and any other unsafe feature the library does not use today, whatever it measures |
| Output edges: `QRCodeData` built from the scorer's packed rows, and the quiet-zone span paths of Standard QR and Micro QR | Micro QR and rMQR kernels. Their placement and Reed-Solomon already run at or under decode speed |
| Benchmarks: quiet-zone-free span rows for every encode benchmark, the mid and long shapes the measurements used, a committed stage harness, and the README images regenerated at the end | Public API. Nothing is added or changed |
| Vector128 and ARM64 tiers of the new scorer, measured on their builds | A tier for a build nobody can measure. It is written when a machine is available |
| Leads measured as ceilings first: Reed-Solomon across blocks, placement written as bits, the small-version scorer's popcount and a 512-bit tier | The decoders. The Alphanumeric and Numeric writers, which had a plan of their own (`standardqr-binary-encoder-plan.md`) that this plan placed in the order; it ran as phase 7 and was folded in |

## What has to stay true

- Every symbol is byte-identical to the current encoder's, for every version, ECC level, segmentation, forced mask and output overload. A scorer returns the same eight penalty scores as the textbook definition, not only the same winner, so ties still go to the lower pattern.
- The span overloads allocate nothing. Per-version tables are built on first use and published as the placement tables are, and a test prints each table's size per version so its growth is visible.
- An index into the ECC table never reads another level's entry. Every entry point validates the level before it reads the content (F21 of the 2.0.0 plan, closed on `main` by #446 with `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` naming `eccLevel`), and the lookup keeps a range check of its own that throws the same.
- No new unsafe feature. The `ExpandBitsAdvSimd` alignment hint stays the library's only `unsafe` method, and `[SkipLocalsInit]` is not used. Under the updated memory safety rules that C# 15 starts in preview, a `stackalloc` without an initializer in a `[SkipLocalsInit]` member is an unsafe operation. In an encoder a read before a write would not fail either: it would put stale stack bytes into a symbol that leaves the process. Zero-initialization keeps such a bug deterministic, and the measured gain of skipping it (1 to 12 % at versions 1 to 10, nothing measurable on larger symbols) does not pay for losing that.
- A new tier ships only on a build where it beats that build's current code, measured on that build, as in the 128-bit tiers round. netstandard2.0 keeps its scalar paths, and everything stays trim and NativeAOT safe.

## Findings that set the order

Each finding has its numbers in the references file.

Mask selection is the encode. It is 66 % of a version 1 encode, 55 % at version 6, 83 % at version 19 and 76 to 81 % at versions 39 and 40. The rest of a version 40-L encode is about 13 µs, under its 16 µs decode. A phase that does not touch mask selection is worth at most the remaining share.

The finder-like windows of rule 3 repeat work. Each window is checked as an 11-term AND chain, forward and backward, in rows and in columns. Both orientations are a four-module light run, which rule 1 already computes, next to a seven-module core, so sharing the two cuts each chain to two ANDs over shared terms. The bits are the same by construction. Measured with the ECC index, the mask stage went to 0.93 to 0.98 at versions 1 to 10, 0.53 to 0.60 at version 19 and 0.72 to 0.86 at versions 39 and 40. The two-word tier (versions 12 to 29) gained the most.

Version selection scans. `QRCodeConstants.GetEccInfo` walks a 160-entry table through `IReadOnlyList<ECCInfo>`, and automatic selection calls it once per version it tries, which is 2.35 µs of a version 40 encode. An index takes 65 ns. Sizing, the planners, Structured Append and the decoder call the same method.

The hot methods zero their stack, and that stays. The single-word mask tier zeroes about 6.5 KB per call, because its buffers are sized for 64 rows whatever the symbol. `[SkipLocalsInit]` on four hot methods gained 8 to 12 % end to end at version 1, 1 to 2 % at versions 6 and 10, and nothing measurable at versions 19 to 40, where the tiers rent their scratch, and it is not used. Sizing the buffers to the symbol, which is safe code, recovered part of that at version 1 (a third on one shape, most of it on the other) and nothing at versions 6 and 10, where a variable-size `stackalloc` zeroes less efficiently than a constant one. Two safe levers were left to measure: a constant 32-row size for versions 1 to 3, and one buffer fewer, with the complement rows computed where they are read. Phase 2 measured both, and together they won (Progress log).

The forced mask path is a per-module loop. `ApplyMaskPattern` evaluates the mask predicate for every module: 28 µs at version 40 for one pattern, where the cached packed templates need about one XOR per 64 modules. In stage timing it is slower than automatic selection only around version 6, which does not reproduce F23's end-to-end figures, so its phase measures F23's shape first. Once mask selection is faster, the forced path would be the slower one at every version.

Row rules on wide rows pay for cross-word shifts, and column rules do not. From version 12 a row spans two or three words, and every shifted term of a row-direction rule pulls bits across them (five shifts and two ORs per term in the three-word tier). Column-direction rules combine whole row words. Holding each candidate also transposed turns every row rule into a column rule on the transpose. Masking is an XOR, so the transposed candidate is the transposed data XOR a per-version transposed template, and the data is transposed once per symbol. The untuned prototype ran mask selection at 0.35 to 0.41 of the current time for versions 20 to 40 and lost below version 12, where a row is one word and the lane-per-pattern tier stays. Its operations are all whole-word and vertical, so it may also give the Vector128 builds a tier for versions 12 to 40, where the current SoA tiers did not beat scalar.

The output edges are a few percent each. The class API packs the byte matrix into bits after the scorer has already held it as bits (46 ns at version 1, 2.8 µs at version 40, 4 to 6 %). The Standard QR span path with a quiet zone rents a buffer, clears the whole destination and copies rows (7 to 8 % at version 1). Micro QR's span path does the same and pays 19 to 23 %, where rMQR writes into the strided window and clears only the margins.

The writers are a ceiling that grows. They are 3.2 to 9.3 % of a single-symbol encode and 3.6 to 4.1 % of the Structured Append sets measured, above the 3 % bar of their plan. Their share roughly doubles once mask selection runs at the prototype's speed, so their plan runs after the scorer phases.

## Relation to the writer plan

`standardqr-binary-encoder-plan.md` ran as phase 7 and was folded into `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` and deleted with it (Progress log). This section is kept as the order it set. That plan and this one changed different code: that plan the Alphanumeric and Numeric writers in `QRBinaryEncoder`, this one mask selection, the ECC table lookup and the output paths. They were written as separate plans, to land in separate PRs, and neither needs the other to be correct; phase 7 then ran on this plan's branch. They meet in three places.

- The ceiling. That plan's gain is bounded by the writers' share of an encode, and mask selection is most of the rest. The share is 3.2 to 9.3 % today and roughly doubles after phase 5, so phase 7 runs that plan then. Run earlier, its end-to-end delta would be measured against a denominator this plan is about to shrink.
- The measurement. Its phase 1 asks for the writers' share by stage timing. The references file answers that for the current code, and this plan's phase 1 commits the stage harness and the long alphanumeric and numeric shapes it needs. Its numbers are taken again when it starts, because phases 2 to 5 move them. Its premise of 2.1 ns a character (63 µs on 30,000 characters) measured about 1.0 ns here (29.7 µs), which is one more reason to re-measure first.
- The fold. Both fold into the Performance section of `specs/standardqr-encoder.md`, so whichever folds second merges into what the first wrote.

Each phase follows the test-first workflow, updates the affected spec in the same change, and appends a Progress log entry with Done / Lessons / benchmark delta. No public API changes. Each phase reports its kernel ratio and end-to-end delta against the previous commit, from interleaved rounds with the same benchmark file, and reads the arms it does not touch as the day's noise.

Phase 1 comes first because every later exit is a delta against it. Phases 2 and 3 are small, already measured (0.64 to 0.97 end to end without any stack change) and checkable by parity tests, so they ship before the large change, and phase 3's tiers become the baseline phase 5 has to beat. Phase 4 precedes phase 5 because a faster automatic path would leave the forced one slower at every version. The writers wait for phase 5 because their ceiling roughly doubles by then.

## Verification notes

- Parity is on scores, not winners. A scorer that picks the right pattern for a wrong reason can pass a winner test, so each tier is compared with a textbook byte-matrix scorer on all eight candidates, on random data and on degenerate data (all light, all dark, stripes along rows and along columns). The prototype passed this on 240 matrices across versions 1 to 40.
- The public API's output over a corpus is hashed in the previous commit and in the change, and each side prints which tree it loaded. The measurement's corpus (7,647 symbols across lengths, alphabets, ECC levels, quiet zones, the class API, Micro QR and rMQR) is the floor.
- Planted faults each fail a test: a finder window offset (the core one module early, the light run at 6 modules instead of 7), a transposed format or version overlay one module off, an ECC table index one version or one level off, and a stack buffer one row shorter than the symbol.
- A/B runs alternate base and change in one session and report the mean of at least two rounds per side. A single short run of the same row moved by up to 30 % during the measurement.
- A stage is compared in the same timing mode on both sides. Run with every other shape interleaved in one process, placement and interleave read 23 to 63 % higher than run alone, while the compute-bound stages and the end-to-end rows did not move.

## Open decisions

None open. Phase 5 settled the two that were here (Progress log): the transposed scorer replaced the two-word and three-word AVX2 tiers outright, since it won at every version 12 to 40, and its tables are the 12-periodic templates ANDed with per-version allowed rows, since full per-pattern tables gained 1 to 4 % for eight times the memory.

## Progress log

Entries are appended per phase: what was done, what was learned, and the benchmark delta or an explicit statement that no hot path moved.

### Phase 1, baseline (2026-10-02)

No hot path moved: the library is unchanged, and only benchmarks, the timing mode and these documents changed.

Done.
- `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd`, `MicroQREncodeEndToEnd` and `RmQREncodeEndToEnd` have a "(Span, QZ0)" row per decode-comparable shape (11, 4 and 4), so each encode row now has a quiet-zone-free twin that compares with its decode row like for like. These rows moved to their own classes on 2026-10-06 (the entry "Benchmark rows aligned across the symbologies"). `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd` has three new shapes: 300 alphanumeric characters (10-M), 4,296 alphanumeric characters (40-L) and 7,089 digits (40-L), with a class row and a quiet-zone-free row each. They are also the long writer shapes `standardqr-binary-encoder-plan.md` asks for.
- The stage harness is the `stage/` shapes of the timing mode in `tests/FeatherQR.AotAnalysis` (`--time --shape stage/`), linked into the WebAssembly report too: 180 shapes over nine Standard QR, three Micro QR and three rMQR symbols. Each symbol has its end-to-end rows (default quiet zone, quiet zone 0, class API) and each stage alone on the input the stage before it produced. The open decision went this way because the timing mode already reaches the internals through its `InternalsVisibleTo`, already holds the mask kernel shapes, and runs on the JIT, NativeAOT and WebAssembly builds phase 6 has to measure. The library's `InternalsVisibleTo` list is unchanged.
- Each symbol's stage composition is checked once against the generator's own matrix, byte for byte, and against the version the shape is named for, and a shape is never built if either fails. A planted fault (version information left out of the composition) stopped the version 40 shapes as it should.
- On `main` the committed harness reproduced the references file's stage table: every end-to-end and mask selection row within 12 %, placement and interleave within 3 % when run alone. The new BenchmarkDotNet rows all run, checked with a dry job, and their first numbers are in the references file ("Phase 1 baseline").
- The timing mode publishes as NativeAOT without trim or AOT warnings and runs the stage shapes there. The WebAssembly report builds with the new file linked. The test suite passes (34,859 tests, 396 skipped).

Lessons.
- The repository's benchmark labels were wrong for two shapes, and the version check found it on its first run. `QR_Byte_V20_M` (620 bytes) encodes version 19-M and `QR_Byte_V40_H` (1,200 bytes) version 39-H, with 77 blocks rather than the 81 a comment claimed, and the timing mode's `encode/qr-v6-url-M` URL fits version 5. Both tiers' boundaries are unaffected (19 and 20 share the two-word tier, 39 and 40 the three-word one), so no conclusion moves. The benchmark comments now name the true versions, the method names stay so earlier results remain comparable, and the references file uses the true versions. A shape that names its version asserts it.
- The timing mode interleaves every selected shape in one process. That leaves compute-bound stages where BenchmarkDotNet puts them but costs memory-bound ones their warm caches (placement and interleave read 23 to 63 % higher). So a stage's change is read against the same stage in the same mode, and a share of an encode from shapes run alone.

### Phase 2, lookups and stack buffers (2026-10-03)

Against `main`, from the timing mode (five interleaved rounds per build, the median of each run's median, quiet zone 0), end to end: version 1-L 0.93, 1-M 0.92, 6-M 0.91, 10-M 0.92, 19-M 0.96 (lowest run median, see Lessons), 39-H 0.93, 40-L 0.96, 40-L alphanumeric 0.97 and 40-L numeric 0.96. Version selection went from 2.40 µs to 65 ns at version 40-L, 544 to 36 ns at 19-M and 73 to 11 ns at 6-M. The single-word mask kernel ran at 0.92 (version 1), 0.95 (6) and 0.97 (10). Micro QR and rMQR, which the phase does not touch, read 1.00 to 1.03, and the untouched version 40 mask kernel 0.98.

Done.
- `QRCodeConstants.GetEccInfo` is an index into a table built in `[version - 1][L, M, Q, H]` order, held in a nested class so it is built on first use after the base values it reads. The version scan also prices the payload once rather than once per version, which took the rest of version 40's selection from about 105 to 65 ns.
- `QRCodeConstantsEccInfoTest` holds the index to its order: all 160 entries against the codeword count of the placement layout, ISO anchors, and versions outside the table.
- F21 was first closed here at the lookup, keeping `ArgumentException` and adding the parameter name. `main` closed it at the same time with #446, which validates the level, the ECI and the quiet zone at every entry point and throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, and the merge took that contract. The lookup's range check stays as an internal guard and throws what the entry points throw, and this phase's own validation test was dropped for #446's route test, which covers the same entry points.
- The AVX2 single-word mask tier allocates 32 rows for versions 1 to 3 and 64 above, and computes the row complements where the column finder windows read them, dropping its third buffer. Measured on their own against Part A (the index alone): the 32-row size helped only versions 1 to 3, the dropped buffer helped versions 1 to 10, and both together were best, 0.93 to 0.94 (version 1), 0.96 (6) and 0.97 (10) end to end, with nothing moving from version 19 up. Each variant matched the scalar scorer in the parity mode before it was timed.
- The corpus hash (7,647 symbols) is unchanged, the parity mode matches, and the test suite passes (34,889 tests, 396 skipped).
- `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` has the indexed lookup and the undefined level's failure under version selection, the decision against `[SkipLocalsInit]`, and two performance lessons.
- Not changed: the Vector128, ARM64 and scalar single-word tiers keep their 64-row buffers. Each needs its own build's measurement, which phase 3 takes for those tiers anyway, so the change moved to phase 3.

Lessons.
- On this machine a whole run of one shape lands in one of two speeds, on either build: version 19-M ran at about 21 µs or at 27 to 29 µs per run, likely from where the process lands on the two-CCD 7950X3D. A median over five runs still flips when two runs on one side land slow, so a change smaller than that gap is read from the lowest run median, from more runs, or with the process pinned to one CCD.
- Background load is bursty here. An early three-round A/B read Part A 50 % slower on a mask kernel it does not touch, and five rounds with run medians put it level. A single round decides nothing.
- Indexing the table left a version-independent cost inside the scan: the payload's bit count was recomputed for every version tried. A loop over versions is read for what does not depend on the version.

### Phase 2 follow-up, the ECC table's build (2026-10-03)

No hot path moved: only the table's one-time build changed, and a lookup still allocates nothing.

Done.
- `CreateCapacityECCTable` fills its 160-entry array in place. Phase 2 kept the old build, a `List<ECCInfo>` grown by a four-entry collection expression per version, and added `ToArray`, so the table's first use allocated 17,360 B for a 5,144 B array: the list's array, 40 temporary arrays with their wrappers (7,040 B), and the copy. It now allocates the array alone, and the first Standard QR encode in a process went from 90,256 to 78,040 B. The retained memory is that array either way, and the `Lazy<T>`, its delegate and the list that phase 2 removed were about 100 B.
- `QRCodeConstantsEccInfoTest` fails on each of five planted faults in the new build: the version or the level label one off, the data one version or one level off, and a field read from its neighbour.

Lessons.
- A table's first-use allocation read against the table's own size shows what its build wastes. Swapping `Lazy<List<T>>` for an array by appending `ToArray` kept the whole list build and added a copy.

### Phase 3, shared finder-window terms (2026-10-03)

Against the commit before, from the timing mode (seven interleaved rounds per build, each process pinned to one CCD, the median of the run medians, quiet zone 0), end to end on the JIT with AVX2: version 1-L 0.96, 1-M 0.94, 6-M 0.94, 10-M 0.97, 19-M 0.52, 39-H 0.71, 40-L 0.75, 40-L alphanumeric 0.76 and 40-L numeric 0.76. The mask kernel ran at 0.92 to 0.94 at versions 1 to 10, 0.40 to 0.42 at versions 12 to 27 and 0.69 to 0.71 at versions 28 and 40, and the scalar tiers at 0.81 to 0.87. On default NativeAOT versions 1 to 10 ran at 0.90 to 0.92 end to end, 19-M at 0.82 and 40-L at 0.83, and on WebAssembly AOT at 0.93 to 0.95, 0.80 and 0.84. Micro QR and rMQR, which the phase does not touch, read 0.98 to 1.03 on every build. The tables are in the references file ("Phase 3").

Done.
- Rule 3 is built from two shared terms in every scorer tier: scalar single- and triple-word, AVX2 single-, two- and three-word, Vector128 and ARM64. In the row direction the core is one AND of six terms and the light run is rule 1's, and the two windows never share a start, so one popcount of their OR counts both. In the column direction each tier writes the light run and the core once per row, into buffers column rule 1 is done with or into the rows themselves, which every caller rebuilds per candidate, and reads each twice. `MatchFinderRow` serves the scalar triple-word tier and the vector tiers' tail rows, and `MatchFinderRow64` the scalar single-word tier and the ARM64 tail, so the AVX2 file's copy is gone.
- The Vector128 tier also lost its complement buffer, phase 2's second change. Measured as three variants on its three builds, that beat the shared terms alone by 2 to 6 % on default NativeAOT and WebAssembly and read level end to end on the JIT without AVX2. The 32-row size won on no 128-bit build and not on the scalar single-word tier, so it ships nowhere new. The scalar single-word tier's complement buffer now holds the light runs, so it has none to drop.
- `ModulePlacerMaskScoreParityTest` compares every tier's score with the textbook score: every single-word size, the two- and three-word tiers at their ends and between, on random matrices at three densities, degenerate ones, windows planted at a row's first and last start and across the 64-bit word boundaries in both orientations, and near misses with one module flipped. It holds the early abort to its contract (the score, or `int.MaxValue` only when the bound is below the score). Its ARM64 cases run on CI's ARM64 legs.
- Planted faults: the core one module early and the light run at 6 modules instead of 7, in each tier's rows and columns and in the vector tiers' scalar tails (28 faults), and two in the Vector128 tier's new column terms. Each fails a test, and each tier's score test catches its own tier's. Three, the tail windows of the two- and three-word AVX2 tiers, fail only the score test.
- The corpus hash (7,647 symbols) is unchanged under the AVX2 tiers, with AVX off and with hardware intrinsics off. The timing mode's parity check matches for every variant on the JIT with and without AVX2, on default NativeAOT and on WebAssembly AOT. The test suite passes (34,949 tests, 402 skipped).
- `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` has the shared terms under mask evaluation, score parity under Validation, two performance lessons, and the 128-bit builds' buffer result beside the stack-zeroing one.
- Not measured: ARM64 is changed the same way, but no ARM64 machine was available, so it was compiled and not run here. Its score cases and `ModulePlacerMaskAdvSimdParityTest` run on CI's ARM64 legs, and its timing waits for a machine.
- From review: the lane scorers' abort is checked lane by lane, with a bound at and one under each lane's score. A lane at or under the bound must read its exact score. Planted, an abort taken when any lane rather than every lane is over the bound passed the old check, which only required exact scores once the bound was above every lane, and only the selection tests caught it. It now fails the score test of both lane scorers.

Lessons.
- Pinning and interleaving do not protect against a burst. A first five-round run had two rounds on which every row of one side, the untouched ones included, read up to 58 % slower. A control shape the change cannot reach, read beside every A/B, tells such a round from a result.
- One buffer change can win on one build and lose on another. Dropping the Vector128 tier's third buffer won on default NativeAOT and WebAssembly and cost its kernel about 3 % on the JIT without AVX2, so a buffer change is measured on each build that runs the tier.
- A shared term gains what it saves. On two-word rows each dropped shift was two shifts and an OR per word, and selection more than halved. On one-word rows a shift is one instruction, and selection moved 6 to 8 %.
- A WebAssembly AOT publish from a deep directory fails. From the scratch directory the emscripten step's paths passed 260 characters, and the publish stopped on a missing compiled-methods file. It worked from a short directory.
- A merge without conflicts can still undo a change. The table build's last line read `return table;` at the merge base and on `main`, so git kept this branch's `return table.ToArray();`, and it compiled because an array is enumerable. A file both sides changed is read after the merge, not trusted for merging cleanly.

### Phase 4, the pinned mask (2026-10-03)

F23's shape first, on `main`: 1,000 characters at M is version 26, and with quiet zone 0 it encoded in 16.0 µs automatic, 34.3 µs with pattern 0 pinned and 33.7 µs with pattern 3, on the JIT with AVX2. The time is `ApplyMaskPattern` itself, the mask predicate tested module by module: 26 µs with the pattern as a variable, where scoring all eight candidates and applying the winner took 9 µs. Against the commit before, from the timing mode (seven interleaved rounds per build, each process pinned to one CCD, the median of the run medians, quiet zone 0), the pinned encode now runs at 0.21 to 0.47 of its time on the JIT with AVX2, and at 0.25 to 0.64 of the automatic encode. Default NativeAOT, WebAssembly AOT and the JIT without AVX2 read 0.24 to 0.69 of the pinned encode's old time and 0.16 to 0.60 of the automatic one. At every version measured, from 1 to 40 and on every build, a pinned mask now encodes faster than the automatic one. Micro QR, rMQR and the automatic selection, which the phase does not touch, read 0.98 to 1.05. The tables are in the references file ("Phase 4").

Done.
- `ApplyMaskPattern` applies the pinned pattern as the selection applies its winner: each row takes the pattern's packed template row, masked to the row's unblocked modules read from the blocked bitmask, and XORs it into the bytes. It dispatches as `MaskCode` does, to AVX2 (32 modules a step), ARM64 AdvSimd (16) or the scalar route (8, SWAR), and each route is internal so a test can enter it on any machine. `AllowedRow64` is the single-word unblocked row, shared with `MaskCode64`. The per-module predicate `ModulePlacer.GetMaskBit`, used by nothing else, is gone. It also refuses a buffer shorter than the matrix, since the wide rows are written through unchecked references.
- `ModulePlacerMaskApplyParityTest` holds `ApplyMaskPattern` and each route to the ISO/IEC 18004 predicates applied module by module, at all 40 versions and all eight patterns, on random, all-light and all-dark data. Planted faults, a template row off, an unblocked row read one bit off, a row unpacked one module short and a padded copy 16 bytes short, each in the scalar and AVX2 routes and in both widths, all fail it (14 faults). The scalar route's faults fail only its own route test, because the dispatch on this machine takes AVX2.
- F23's shape is a stage symbol of the timing mode (`stage/qr-v26-byte-M/`), every Standard QR symbol has pinned encode rows (`e2e-qz0-mask0`, `e2e-qz0-mask3`) and a pattern 0 row beside the pattern 3 one, and `kernel/MaskForced-vN` sits beside `kernel/MaskCode-vN` at the same eight versions.
- The 7,647-symbol corpus and a 6,504-symbol pinned-mask corpus (versions 1 to 40, every level, every pattern, two contents, quiet zone 0 and 4, the class API) hash the same before and after, under the AVX2 tiers, with AVX off and with hardware intrinsics off. The test suite passes (35,271 tests, 482 skipped).
- The timing mode's parity check (`--parity`) holds the pinned path too, so the builds no test run reaches check it: the dispatch, the route the build takes, against the decoder's mask predicate at every version and pattern. It matches on the JIT with and without AVX2, default NativeAOT and WebAssembly AOT. A template row planted one off in the scalar route failed it with 77 mismatches on the build that takes that route and passed on the AVX2 one.
- After phase 5 the forced path stays the cheaper one: the transposed prototype selected at 7.76 to 20.9 µs for versions 20 to 40, where the pinned kernel takes 0.91 to 3.06 µs, and versions 1 to 11 keep their tier.
- F23 is closed in the 2.0.0 plan, so phase 10 no longer lists it. `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` says how a pinned mask is applied, has the pinned matrices under Validation, and two performance lessons. `specs/standardqr-spec-map.md` lists this test and phase 3's score test beside the other mask tests.
- Not measured: the ARM64 route uses the unpack helpers the ARM64 tier already applies its winner with, but no ARM64 machine was available, so it was compiled and not run here. Its route test runs on CI's ARM64 legs.

Lessons.
- A stage row that passes a literal where the caller passes a variable can time another program. The forced row gave the pattern as a constant, the JIT inlined the call and folded the predicate for that pattern, and the row read half of what an encode paid, so F23 reproduced end to end and not in the stage table. The forced rows now take the pattern as a captured variable, and with it the stage and the end-to-end delta agree.
- A rare option can cost more than the default path it skips. Selection had been optimized round after round on packed rows while the pinned path kept its per-module loop, and at most versions skipping the scoring was slower than doing it.
- The two-word sizes pay for their row tails: version 27's 125 columns leave 29 modules after the last 32-module step and took 1.98 µs, version 28's 129 leave one and took 1.50 µs. At these sizes it is not worth a change, but the same tail is in the selection's winner apply.

### Phase 5, the transposed scorer (2026-10-04)

Against `main`, from the timing mode (nine interleaved rounds per build on the JIT with AVX2, each process pinned to one CCD with the .NET build servers shut down, the median of the run medians), mask selection took 0.82 to 0.90 of its time at versions 12 to 27 and 0.36 to 0.44 at 28 to 40, at every one of the 29 versions. End to end at quiet zone 0: version 19-M 0.92, 26-M 0.90, 39-H 0.51, 40-L 0.54, 40-L alphanumeric 0.61 and 40-L numeric 0.57. On NativeAOT built for x86-64-v3, by the lowest run medians, 0.83 to 0.92 and 0.30 to 0.34, and end to end 0.93 at versions 19 and 26, 0.40 at 39-H and 0.44 at 40-L. The rows the phase does not touch read 0.96 to 1.01. The per-version table is in the references file ("Phase 5").

Done.
- `ModulePlacer.Masking.Transposed.X86.cs` is the AVX2 tier for versions 12 to 40, grown from the prototype in references. Each candidate is held as row word planes and as column word planes (the transpose), so every penalty rule runs along consecutive words of a plane, four per vector, and only the 2x2 rule shifts, by one bit across words. The data is packed and transposed once per symbol, in 64x64 blocks by a vectorized recursive swap. A candidate is the packed planes XOR the pattern's 12-periodic template ANDed with the version's allowed rows and columns, with its format information set in both orientations, and the version information goes into the rows before the transpose. One checkpoint before the column planes' finder windows skips them for a candidate already above the best total.
- It replaced the two-word and three-word SoA tiers outright, which settles the first open decision, so `MaskCode128Simd`, `MaskCode192Simd`, their scorers and their helpers are gone, with the score tests of those two scorers. `PokeFormatBitsSoA2` and `PokeFormatBitsSoA3` moved to the ARM64 file, their only user. The ARM64 tiers are unchanged (phase 6).
- Each choice was measured against its alternative: full per-pattern tables gained 1 to 4 % for about eight times the memory, so the periodic form ships, which settles the second open decision. The prototype's scalar transpose was 7 to 16 % slower. No checkpoint was 0 to 7 % slower, and a checkpoint after the row planes 0 to 6 %, because it almost never fires. An abort check after each row word read level with one check.
- Tables per version, built on first use and published as the other per-version tables are: 4,128 bytes for versions 12 to 26, 4,640 at 27, 9,264 for 28 to 39 and 9,456 at 40, plus 4,608 bytes of template planes shared by all versions. `ModulePlacerMaskTransposedParityTest.Tables_StayUnderTheirBudget` prints them and holds each under 10 KB. Each call rents 12.5 to 25.3 KB of scratch from the array pool and returns it.
- `ModulePlacerMaskTransposedParityTest` holds every candidate's score to the textbook score at all 29 versions and every ECC level, on random, all-light, all-dark and row- and column-striped data. It holds the checkpoint to the abort contract at a bound of each score and one under, the winner and the matrix to the scalar kernel, and refuses a size, a version or a buffer the cache must not see. Of 17 planted faults in the tier (the transpose's masks and lanes, a block one row off, padding read as modules, a format or version module one off in one orientation, the 2x2 carry between words, the template phase, the core, the valid masks, the dark count, the abort taking a tie, the row padding left dirty, the masking pass short), 16 fail it. The abort tie first survived, because the one fixture its test used had row finder windows in every candidate, and fails since the bounds run over every fixture. The short masking pass is equivalent: everything read past it is ANDed with a zero padding row inside it.
- The corpus hashes (7,647 symbols, and 6,504 pinned-mask symbols) are unchanged under the AVX2 tiers, with AVX off and with hardware intrinsics off. The timing mode's parity check matches on the JIT and on NativeAOT for x86-64-v3. The test suite passes (35,797 tests, 482 skipped).
- The timing mode has a mask kernel shape for every version 12 to 40.
- `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` describes the tier under mask evaluation and has two performance lessons, and the spec map lists the file and its test.

Lessons.
- A pass over padded storage stops where the reads stop. The masking pass first covered whole 64-row blocks, twice the symbol at version 12, and stopping it nine entries past the symbol took versions 12 to 27 from 0.90 to 1.00 of phase 3 to about 0.82.
- A checkpoint is worth what is left after it. After the row planes half the score is left, and a candidate whose half already exceeds the best whole total is rare, so it read level with none. Before the last finder windows little is left, and it gained 2 to 6 % at versions 12 to 27.
- Build servers left running belong to the background load. An A/B run read medians up to 1.7 times its lowest run, with the compiler server holding 2.4 GB after the builds. With `dotnet build-server shutdown` before each run, the medians matched the lowest.
- A source file is named for the instruction family it uses. The tier first sat in `ModulePlacer.Masking.Transposed.cs`, and `SimdLayoutTest` refused its AVX2 calls there.

### Phase 6, the transposed scorer on 128-bit builds (2026-10-05)

Against the scalar kernel the 128-bit builds ran for versions 12 to 40, from the timing mode (each process pinned to one CCD with the .NET build servers shut down, the median of the run medians), the 128-bit transposed tier took 0.41 to 0.44 of its mask selection time at versions 12 to 27 and 0.61 to 0.63 at 28 to 40 on the JIT without AVX2, 0.44 to 0.48 and 0.64 to 0.67 on default NativeAOT, 0.50 to 0.59 and 0.68 to 0.71 on WebAssembly AOT, and 0.39 to 0.45 and 0.56 to 0.58 interpreted, at every one of the 29 versions. End to end at quiet zone 0, against `main` (5444c64) in alternating rounds, version 19-M took 0.49 to 0.61 of its time across the four builds, 26-M 0.48 to 0.59, 39-H 0.64 to 0.76, 40-L 0.64 to 0.77, 40-L alphanumeric 0.69 to 0.80 and 40-L numeric 0.63 to 0.77, WebAssembly AOT gaining the least. The rows the phase does not touch read 0.99 to 1.04, and the pinned-mask encodes 1.00 to 1.03. The per-version table is in the references file ("Phase 6").

Done.
- `ModulePlacer.Masking.Transposed.Vector128.cs` is phase 5's scorer on 128-bit vectors, two rows or columns per vector: the same planes, tables, rules and checkpoint. Popcounts go into the 16-bit accumulators of the single-word 128-bit tier and reduce only at the checkpoint and at the end of a candidate, and the 64-bit lane shifts are WebAssembly's own there, as in that tier. The transpose pairs whole vectors down to the 2-row swap and swaps the two lanes of a vector for the 1-row swap. The winner goes into the matrix through the scalar tier's unpack.
- `MaskCodeVector128` takes it for versions 12 to 40, on x64 without AVX2 and on WebAssembly, in place of the scalar kernel. It ships on all four 128-bit builds, since it won on each at every version.
- The tables, the template planes, the version and format overlays and the winner's delta moved to `ModulePlacer.Masking.Transposed.cs`, which has no vector code and is shared by both tiers. The AVX2 file keeps its vector code, otherwise unchanged.
- ARM64 is not written. No ARM64 machine was at hand, and the scope leaves out a tier nobody can measure, so ARM64 keeps its SoA tiers for versions 12 to 40 until one is. One was later, and ARM64 took the tier (the follow-up below).
- `ModulePlacerMaskTransposedParityTest` runs each of its tests on both routes, AVX2 and 128-bit, each entered directly, so an x64 machine with AVX2 runs both. `ModulePlacerMaskVector128ParityTest` holds the 128-bit dispatch to the scalar kernel at versions 12, 27, 28 and 40 too. The timing mode's parity check now covers every version 1 to 40 through the dispatch and the 128-bit tier entered directly, and matches on the JIT with and without AVX, on default NativeAOT, and on WebAssembly AOT and interpreted. Of 25 planted faults, all fail it: 22 in the 128-bit tier (the transpose's masks, its lane swap and a block one row off, each step of the row packer, the template phase, the scratch padding read as modules by each rule, a run, core or window offset one off, the 2x2 carry, the dark count taken twice, the abort taking a tie, one lane dropped from the reduction, the column finder windows one entry off, the winner's template row) and 3 in the shared tables (a format or version module one off, the row padding left dirty).
- The corpus hashes (7,647 symbols, and 6,504 pinned-mask symbols) are unchanged under the AVX2 tiers, with AVX off, where their versions 12 to 40 now run through the new tier, and with hardware intrinsics off. The test suite passes (35,981 tests, 482 skipped), and with AVX off, where every encode of versions 12 to 40 takes the new tier (928 skipped).
- The timing mode has a scalar and a 128-bit kernel shape for every version 12 to 40 (`kernel/MaskCode-vN-scalar`, `kernel/MaskCode-vN-v128`).
- `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` has the 128-bit tier under mask evaluation and its numbers in the performance lesson on the transposed scorer, and the spec map lists the two files and the tests.

Lessons.
- A layout that loses on a build is not a verdict on that build's vectors. The SoA scorers ported to 128-bit vectors in the 128-bit tiers round (2026-09-30) lost to the scalar kernel, by up to 5.8 times on WebAssembly, and versions 12 to 40 stayed scalar there. The transposed tier on the same vectors, with no cross-word shift but the 2x2 rule's one bit, took 0.39 to 0.71 of the scalar time on every 128-bit build, the interpreter included. Why the SoA scorers lost there was not measured.
- A ratio against a fixed-width baseline steps where the new code changes width. The scalar kernel works on three words at every version from 12, so it shows no step at version 28. The transposed tier pays for the words a row has, so its time grows by 41 to 47 % from version 27 to 28 and its ratio rises from 0.41 to 0.51 to 0.57 to 0.71 across the four builds.

### Phase 7, the writers (2026-10-05)

`standardqr-binary-encoder-plan.md` ran as written, its four phases in order, and is deleted. Its decisions and lessons are folded into `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` ("Build the data codewords", Performance), and its measurements into the references file ("Phase 7: the writers").

Against `main` (9897279), from the stage harness (alternating rounds, each process pinned to one CCD with the .NET build servers shut down, the median of the run medians), the change took a version 40 encode to 0.92 to 0.93 of its time on the JIT with and without AVX2 and on default NativeAOT. A version 40 alphanumeric encode went to 0.83 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.86 interpreted, a version 40 numeric one to 0.96 to 0.97 there. A version 10 alphanumeric encode went to 0.84 to 0.96, the 30,000-character alphanumeric set to 0.91 to 0.97 and the 50,000-digit set to 0.95 to 1.00. The payload alone took 0.12 to 0.20 of its time at version 40 alphanumeric and 0.25 to 0.43 numeric. The version 1 symbols read 0.96 to 1.00 end to end, and the rows the change does not touch 0.96 to 1.03.

Done.
- Phase 1 (measure). The stage harness has a payload row for every Standard QR symbol and two Structured Append sets of one mode. The writers were 6.4 to 13.0 % of a version 40 encode on x64 and 6.6 to 21.8 % on WebAssembly, and only the version 1 symbols fell under the plan's 3 % bar, on some builds, so phases 2 and 3 went ahead.
- Phase 2 (Alphanumeric). A portable writer packs four pairs into one 44-bit append through `BitWriter.WriteWide`, the one addition to the type, and checks a step by one OR over `CharacterSets`' value table, whose -1 marks a character outside the alphabet. x64 has an SSE4.1 tier: sixteen characters a step, the rMQR writer's form on one pack of two loads, a membership table over the low nibble, the loop on a local copy of the writer, then one step of eight. WebAssembly has the same steps on its SIMD, with dot products for the multiply-adds. A run under eight characters is written in place. A character outside the alphabet still throws `ArgumentException` at that character, after the fields of the pairs ahead of it, through the old per-character loop, which is not inlined.
- Phase 3 (Numeric). A portable writer takes fifteen digits from five 8-byte loads, each multiply giving one group, then nine an append. x64 has an SSSE3 tier: twelve digits from one pack of sixteen chars and a pshufb layout, on a local copy of the writer. WebAssembly keeps the portable writer, and a run under sixteen digits is written in place.
- Refuted, with their numbers in the references file: an AVX2 tier for either writer; the portable Vector128 form on x64 (0.41 of the old writer against 0.23); the rMQR writer's SSE4.1 Numeric form (0.38 against 0.30); WebAssembly's Numeric step (0.95 of the portable writer AOT-compiled, up to 1.65 interpreted); the local writer copy in the portable loops. ARM64 ran the portable writers, measured there in the follow-up below, until its NEON steps shipped after the review.
- `QRBinaryEncoderPayloadParityTest` holds the portable and x64 tiers to the payload written from the definition. It covers lengths 0 to 300 at every starting alignment and long runs at every fifth, every character outside the alphabet up to 0xFF and some past it in the lanes of a vector step, runs as slices of a longer text, and runs that end at a protected page (`PageEndMemory`). The timing mode's parity check holds every tier a build runs to the old writers, WebAssembly's included. `SimdTiers` and the generated table in `qrcode-simd-tiers.md` have the two writers.
- 26 faults were planted in the writers and `BitWriter.WriteWide`. 21 fail a test, two crash the test host on the protected page (reads past the run; the mutation tool then listed a crashed run as not caught, and counts it as a catch since), and three are equivalent by construction: a length guard that only decides whether to copy the writer, a right shift no -1 survives, and a 64-bit end that leaves 32 bits pending, which every `BitWriter` path handles.
- The corpus hashes are unchanged under the AVX2 tiers, with AVX off and with hardware intrinsics off. That covers the 7,647 symbols, the 6,504 pinned-mask symbols, and a new pass of 980 mixed-mode encodes and Structured Append sets. The test suite passes (36,043 tests, 482 skipped), with AVX off (928 skipped) and with hardware intrinsics off (1,731 skipped).

Lessons (the spec has each with its numbers).
- The ceiling moved with the denominator. At version 40 the Alphanumeric writer was 5.5 % of the encode before the mask work and 13.0 % after it on the JIT, and a fifth of it on WebAssembly.
- A method's inlining budget is spent by what it inlines. The portable writer, in a body whose throwing path still sat in its loop, inlined into its entry lost its 8-byte store to a call and read 1.64 times the old writer's time at 16 characters. Compiled on its own it read 0.77.
- A load wider than what it uses is guarded by its loop bound alone, and no output can show it reading past the run; only a protected page did.
- A tier's numbers come from the build that runs it. On WebAssembly AOT the harness's copy of the old writer ran 1.5 times slower than the library's own, so only the base-against-change A/B gives that build's delta.

### Phase 7 follow-up, the writers on ARM64 (2026-10-05)

Phase 7 ran without an ARM64 machine, and this measured it on an Apple M2 (osx-arm64, .NET 10.0.12). Against `main` (9897279), with the phase's stage harness on both sides (nine alternating rounds per build, one process each, the median of the run medians), the change took a version 40 alphanumeric encode to 0.96 of its time on the JIT and on default NativeAOT, a version 40 numeric one to 0.93 and 0.95, a version 10 alphanumeric one to 0.92 and 0.94 and the two Structured Append sets to 0.96 to 0.97. The payload alone took 0.24 to 0.36 of its time from 300 characters up. The version 1 symbols read 0.94 to 1.01, where the payload is under 2 % of the encode, and the rows the change does not touch 0.98 to 1.01. No code path changed. The tables are in the references file ("Phase 7: the writers", ARM64).

Done.
- The test suite passes on ARM64 (18,111 tests on net10.0 with 346 skipped, 18,098 on net8.0 with 335 skipped), the payload tests' portable route included and their x64 route skipped. The timing mode's parity check matches on the JIT and on NativeAOT, the payload writers included, and `--simd-class arm64` holds both writers to `Scalar`.
- Phase 1 of the writer plan, on ARM64: with the old writers the payload was 7.0 to 8.2 % of a version 40 encode and 7.9 to 8.2 % at version 10, above the 3 % bar as on every other build. The old writers ran slower than on x64 (1.69 ns a character, 1.06 ns a digit) and the portable ones no slower, so the portable writers took 0.24 to 0.36 of the old writers' time from 300 characters up, against 0.44 to 0.66 on x64. After them the payload is at most 3.2 % of an encode.
- A NEON step, measured against the portable writers by BenchmarkDotNet on the JIT: eight Alphanumeric and six Numeric variants, each held to the old writers' stream first. The best took 0.38 to 0.41 of the portable Alphanumeric writer's time and 0.55 to 0.58 of the Numeric one's from 300 characters up. With the shares above that would save 0.7 to 2.0 % of an encode, by estimate, and a step taking no time at most 3.2 %. It did not ship then, and ARM64 kept the portable writers. With the transposed scorer the shares crossed the bar, and the steps shipped after an end-to-end run ("ARM64 checks after the review", below). The prototypes are described in the references file.
- `SimdTiers` gives the measured reason for ARM64's `Scalar` cells, and `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` has the ARM64 numbers in place of "no ARM64 machine was at hand".

Lessons.
- The writers' ceiling on ARM64 waited on its scorer. ARM64 then ran the SoA scorers for versions 12 to 40 (phase 6), and mask selection was 77 to 79 % of a version 40 encode there (72.6 of 92.3 µs on the JIT, 63.9 of 82.5 µs on NativeAOT), so the same writer was a small share. With mask selection at the 0.4 of its time the transposed tier reached on AVX2, the encode would be about 49 µs and the NEON step would save about 2.8 % (an estimate from the stage rows), so the step was to be measured again once ARM64 had that scorer. It got the scorer in the next follow-up, and the step was measured end to end after the review (below).
- A ratio measured on one build does not carry to another. The same portable Alphanumeric writer took a third of the old writer's time on the M2 and two thirds on the x64 JIT: the old writer ran 1.5 times slower a character there and the portable one about a quarter faster.
- At tens of nanoseconds a process decides more than a variant on this Mac. The canary, the portable writer's own code, read 1.79 times the baseline at 40 digits in one round and 0.99 in the other, so a short-run verdict there needs two rounds that agree.

### Phase 6 follow-up, the transposed scorer on ARM64 (2026-10-05)

On an Apple M2 (osx-arm64, .NET 10.0.12), against `encode4` (a740295) in alternating rounds, mask selection took 0.87 to 0.98 of its time at versions 12 to 27 and 0.42 to 0.57 at 28 to 40, on the JIT and default NativeAOT, at every version. End to end at quiet zone 0: version 19-M 0.89 and 0.93, 26-M 0.88 and 0.92, 39-H 0.55 and 0.63, 40-L 0.55 to 0.56 and 0.60 to 0.63 (byte, alphanumeric, numeric), the class API at 40-L 0.58 and 0.64, the 30,000-character set 0.64 and 0.70. The rows the change does not touch read 0.97 to 1.02. The tables are in the references file ("Phase 6", ARM64).

Done.
- `MaskCodeAdvSimd` takes versions 12 to 40 to `MaskCodeTransposedAdvSimd` in `ModulePlacer.Masking.Arm64.cs`: the 128-bit tier's masking, rules and checkpoint, unchanged, with the NEON tier's sixteen-module row packing and winner unpack. The 128-bit popcount is NEON's cnt and uadalp on ARM64, a branch the other builds compile away. Their code is unchanged: the 128-bit file only gained a sentence in its summary.
- The two- and three-word SoA tiers, their scorers, packers and format overlays are gone, and the ARM64 file is about 590 lines shorter. The score tests of the two scorers went with them. Versions 1 to 11 keep the single-word NEON tier.
- `ModulePlacerMaskTransposedParityTest` has an ARM64 route beside the AVX2 and 128-bit ones, entered directly: scores against the textbook, the abort contract and the selection against the scalar kernel at all 29 versions. Of 7 planted faults (the popcount dropping a bit, a row packed one module short, the third word not stored, the version information left out, the column padding left dirty, the winner's template phase, the winner's pattern), all fail the mask tests, and none only one method.
- The timing mode's parity check matches on the JIT and NativeAOT. 4,832 Standard QR symbols hash the same before and after and with hardware intrinsics off. The test suite passes on ARM64 (18,197 tests on net10.0 with 346 skipped, 18,184 on net8.0 with 335 skipped).
- `specs/standardqr-encoder.md` says ARM64 runs the transposed tier and has its numbers in the lesson on the transposed scorer, and the spec map lists the route and its test.
- The writers' share grew with the shorter encode, by a first run of three rounds to 4.2 to 4.3 % of a version 40 alphanumeric encode and 3.5 to 3.7 % of a numeric one. The NEON step's saving was then only estimated from its kernel ratio, never measured end to end. Both were taken properly after the review ("ARM64 checks after the review", below), where the shares are a table in the references file.

Lessons.
- A portable tier on a new build pays for its fallbacks. As it stood, the 128-bit tier ran on ARM64 at 1.24 to 1.39 of the SoA tiers' time at versions 12 to 27, with a SWAR popcount, movemask packing and an eight-module unpack. NEON's popcount alone took it to 0.89 to 1.01, and the NEON tier's packing and unpack to 0.85 to 0.96. Measured against what it would replace, the same code moved from a loss to a win by three helpers.
- A speedup written beside a dispatch goes stale with the code under it. The comment gave the ARM64 tiers 1.15 to 1.2 times the scalar paths at versions 12 to 40, from before phase 3's shared terms. Measured now (on the Apple M2, 2026-10-05; those runs' tables against the scalar paths are not in the references file), the two-word tier ran at 4.3 to 5 times and the three-word one at 1.6 to 1.9 times, stepping by 2.9 times at version 28, so the transposed tier's gain was mostly that step: 0.42 to 0.57 at 28 to 40 against 0.87 to 0.98 below it.

### From review of phases 7 and the ARM64 follow-ups (2026-10-05)

An adversarial review of the branch, each claim put to three verifiers, left no wrong output for valid input. It left one performance fault, a missed gain, gaps in the checks, and comments and figures the code or the record did not bear out.

Done.
- The transposed tier's one-row lane swap called the software `Vector128.Shuffle` on .NET 8, its index being a local the .NET 8 JIT does not see as a constant (the disassembly had two calls a row pair; .NET 10 emitted `vpermilpd`). The index is now written at each call. On .NET 8 x64 without AVX2 mask selection through the dispatch took 0.88 to 0.92 of its time at versions 12 to 40. ARM64 took this code in its transposed tier and was measured on .NET 10 only, and its .NET 8 builds were measured after the review (below).
- The SSSE3 Numeric step runs from 40 digits. Below that it ran once or twice and took 1.08 to 1.22 of the portable writer's time at 16 to 24 and at 32 digits, on the JIT with and without AVX2 and on default NativeAOT; from 40 it took 0.77 to 1.00. The record had no point between 12 and 40.
- The timing mode's parity check now writes every run also as a slice of a longer text whose next characters are in the alphabet, and holds `CharacterSets`' value table to the alphabet, since the old writers read it too. A run alone ends at the string's terminator, outside the alphabet, so a vector step one short in its loop bound read past the run and still matched; with the slices that fault reads 192 mismatches on x64 and on WebAssembly, where this check is the only one of its tier.
- The SWAR popcount of the 128-bit tier, which no CI leg reaches through the dispatch once ARM64 counts with NEON, is `AddPopCountSwar`, held directly by a test beside the count each build takes. Two planted faults in it fail that test.
- `SimdTiersTest` can scope a kernel to its dispatch method (`file#Method`). The two writers dispatch in one file, and a Numeric dispatch reading no flag passed while `SimdTiers` declared its SSSE3 tier; it now fails.
- `tools/mutation_check.cs` reads a crashed host's stack from stderr alone, passes over an assertion's frames, names an async test by its state machine, reads a stack overflow, deletes a run's old TRX first, stops on a framework failure or an exit code that is not a crash, and has `report`, `evaluate` and `compare` mark what only a crash caught. Each case was crashed on purpose in a copy: a direct read past a protected page, the same inside a delegate assertion through a helper and directly, after an await, a stack overflow, a crash among 2,000 failing cases, and a filter the framework cannot parse.
- Comments and specs re-derived from the code and the record: the Numeric writer's handling of a non-digit, the Alphanumeric path to the throwing writer, the WebAssembly tier's one step, `BitWriter`'s 32-bit stores, the ARM64 header's early exit and reduction, a file name that did not exist, the AVX2 ratios in `SimdTiers`, the NEON step's saving (at most 2.7 % at version 40 alphanumeric, 1.7 % numeric, more than the 0.1 to 0.3 % the steps declined on the other builds would have saved, where the spec had it under them; an estimate, measured end to end in the ARM64 checks below), the mask share on ARM64 (77 to 79 %), the payload test's coverage (the portable and x64 tiers, every alignment to 300 characters and every fifth beyond), the scalar-tier counts in `qrcode-symbologies.md`, the ARM64 scorer sentence in `qrcode-simd-tiers.md`, this plan's writer-plan sentences and the references file's header. The inlining figure is recorded: the shipped body inlined reads 0.81 of the old writer against 0.71 at 16 characters, and the 1.64 of the phase was an earlier body.
- The corpus hashes are unchanged under AVX2, with AVX off and with hardware intrinsics off (the 7,647 symbols, the 6,504 pinned-mask symbols, the 980 mixed and Structured Append encodes). The test suite passes (36,223 tests, 654 skipped; with AVX off 1,100 skipped), and the timing mode's parity check matches on the JIT with and without AVX2, default NativeAOT, and WebAssembly AOT and interpreted.

Lessons.
- A tier taken over by a new build carries the old one's runtime behaviour as well as its rules. The 128-bit transposed code ran its lane swap through the software `Shuffle` on .NET 8 since phase 6, a cost no .NET 10 measurement shows, and ARM64 inherited it with the code.
- A vector step's cut-over is measured where the step runs once or twice. The Numeric step was sent every run from 16 digits on the strength of 500 and 7,089, and lost to the portable writer at 16 to 24 and at 32 digits, won at 28, and at 36 read 1.00 on the JIT and 1.07 on NativeAOT.
- A parity check over whole strings cannot see a read past the run, because the terminator stops a vector step as a bad character does. A run has to be checked as a plan passes it, as a slice whose next characters the step would accept.

### ARM64 checks after the review (2026-10-05)

The review ran without an ARM64 machine and left four questions for one. What does the lane swap's fix do on ARM64's .NET 8 builds? What is the payload's share with the transposed scorer, which the record gave in prose only? Do the NEON writer steps gain end to end now that the encode is shorter, when the record had only their kernel ratio times the share? And is the 3 % bar on the share or on the estimated saving, which the specs read both ways? Measured on the Apple M2 against `encode4` (0fda781). The tables are in the references file ("Phase 6", ARM64, and "Phase 7", ARM64).

Done.
- The lane swap on .NET 8, read in the library's own `Transpose64Vector128`: NativeAOT 8 made two calls to the software `Shuffle` a row pair, and the JIT inlined it, reading each lane back through the stack. After the fix both emit two `tbl`. Mask selection at versions 12 to 40 took 0.90 to 0.98 of its time on NativeAOT 8, the median 0.93, and 0.93 to 1.01 on the JIT, inside the drift of the versions that have no transpose (0.96 to 0.98). The comment at the fix says how each compiler falls back.
- The payload's share with the transposed scorer, nine alternating rounds: 4.2 % of a version 40 alphanumeric encode and 3.5 % of a numeric one, against 2.4 to 2.6 % and 1.9 to 2.1 % with the SoA scorers, 2.9 to 3.1 % at version 10, and 3.0 and 2.6 % of the two sets.
- The bar is on the share, as the tier inventory's rules, this plan's writer phase and the rMQR encoder record apply it. `qrcode-symbologies.md` says so in the rules, and its lesson on bounding a step's gain now says the bound ranks candidates and is not the bar.
- Both NEON steps ship (`QRBinaryEncoder.Arm64.cs`): sixteen characters a step and then one of eight, where one TBL over 64 bytes gives each character's value plus one and 0 outside the alphabet, and fifteen digits from sixteen chars. They take 0.40 to 0.43 and 0.57 to 0.61 of the portable writers' time from 300 characters up on .NET 10. End to end, eighteen rounds on .NET 10 put the alphanumeric encodes at 0.95 to 0.98 and the numeric ones at 0.98 to 1.00, and five on .NET 8 at 0.97 to 0.99 and 0.98 to 1.01. The rows the change does not touch read 0.97 to 1.02, but for the version 1 alphanumeric row on .NET 8, where no step runs: 1.03 to 1.04 there, and 1.01 in nine rounds of its own. The stage rows give a saving of 2.5 % at version 40 alphanumeric on .NET 10 and 1.9 % on .NET 8.
- On .NET 8 the steps start later: from 32 characters and 160 digits, against 8 and 40 on .NET 10 (`AlphanumericAdvSimdMinimum`, `NumericAdvSimdMinimum`). .NET 8 keeps the step's local copy of the writer on the stack, so its steps took 0.60 to 0.64 and 0.70 to 0.82 of the portable writers' time on long runs, and the Numeric step lost up to 48 digits.
- `SimdTiers` has `AdvSimd` in both writers' ARM64 cells with the measured reasons, and the generated table in `qrcode-simd-tiers.md` follows. `QRBinaryEncoderPayloadParityTest` has an ARM64 route entered directly, and the timing mode's parity check and writer shapes take the NEON steps. Of 24 faults planted in the steps (a loop bound one short, a membership check that never stops, three table entries and the index offset, saturation dropped from the narrowing, the multipliers, shifts, lane indexes and digit offset, the step's advance, the local writer not stored back), all fail `QRBinaryEncoderPayloadParityTest`, the three reads past the run by crashing the host at its protected page.
- 5,359 Standard QR symbols hash the same before and after on .NET 8 and .NET 10, and with hardware intrinsics off: the 4,832-symbol corpus of phase 6's ARM64 follow-up, 480 mixed-mode encodes of runs of 1 to 40 characters under `QRSegmentation.Optimal`, and Structured Append sets of one mode and of mixed content under both segmentations.
- The test suite passes on ARM64 (18,206 tests on net10.0 with 346 skipped, 18,193 on net8.0 with 335 skipped), and the timing mode's parity check matches on the JIT and NativeAOT of .NET 8 and .NET 10.
- The specs follow: `standardqr-encoder.md` (the writers' tiers, a lesson rewritten and one added), the spec map (the file and the test's route), `qrcode-symbologies.md` (the bar, the scalar-cell counts, the lesson on a step's bound).

Left open.
- The x64 steps keep the same local copy of the writer and were timed on .NET 10 only, so their gain on .NET 8 is not known. This machine has no x64 runtime to measure it.

Lessons.
- An estimate has to be recorded as one. "Not measured again" read as though the step had been measured end to end once, when the only figure was the share times one less the kernel ratio.
- A bar needs one quantity. The tier inventory and the writer plan applied 3 % to the share, and one lesson applied it to the bound on a step's saving. At a share of 4.2 % and a bound of 2.5 %, the two readings gave opposite answers.
- A gain the size of the spread is sized by the stage rows. Two runs of nine rounds read 0.95 to 0.96 and 0.98 to 1.00 for the same steps at version 40 alphanumeric, while the payload row over the encode gave 2.5 % both times.
- One fix can cost differently on two compilers of one release. NativeAOT 8 called the software `Shuffle` and the JIT inlined it, so the same fix gained 7 % on one and nothing measurable on the other.
- A step's cut-over belongs to a runtime, not only to a build class. .NET 10 promotes the writer's copy to registers and .NET 8 keeps it in memory, so the same step won from 40 digits on one and from 160 on the other.

### Benchmark rows aligned across the symbologies (2026-10-06)

No hot path moved: only the benchmark project and this plan changed.

Done.
- The "(Span, QZ0)" rows moved out of the three encode classes into `QRCodeQuietZone0Encode`, `MicroQRQuietZone0Encode` and `RmQRQuietZone0Encode`, so the encode classes time the path a caller takes by default. Each new class has one row per "(Span)" row of its encode class, under the description the row had before. Phase 8's exit names the classes.
- The rows that ran another symbology for scale left the encode and decode classes.
- Every encode and decode class orders its rows by mode (numeric, alphanumeric, byte, Kanji) within each group, and its summary the same way. `MicroQREncodeEndToend` is now `MicroQREncodeEndToEnd`.
- rMQR rows fit their version as the Standard QR and Micro QR rows do, and "(Pinned)" rows (R11x27 numeric, R17x139 byte and Kanji) take the path that resolves it first. The area fit puts 12 digits in R11x27 and 43 alphanumeric characters in R15x43 (297 and 645 modules, against 301 for R7x43 and 649 for R11x59), so those rows and their decode rows are named for the symbols they write. The payloads are unchanged, so they no longer fill their symbols (R11x27-M holds 14 digits, R15x43-M 46 characters).
- `RmQR_Numeric_AutoFit_Encode` is gone: the fitted numeric row is the same call.

Lessons.
- A comparison row has to write the symbol of the row it is read against. The automatic-fit row was read against the R7x43 baseline but wrote R11x27, so the difference was never the fit's cost alone.

### Phase 8, output edges (2026-10-06)

Against `main` (1df5b10), from the stage harness (alternating rounds, each process pinned to one CCD with the .NET build servers shut down, the median of the run medians, five rounds on the JIT and NativeAOT and three on WebAssembly), the span encode with a quiet zone took 0.84 to 0.94 of its time for Micro QR on the JIT with AVX2, default NativeAOT and WebAssembly AOT, 0.88 to 0.90 on the JIT without AVX2 in runs of Micro QR alone, and 0.98 to 1.02 interpreted. Standard QR's took 0.87 to 0.96 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.96 to 1.01 elsewhere, rMQR's 0.95 to 1.02 but for one interpreted symbol at 1.09, whose quiet-zone-free row read 1.06 in the same run. The class API of Standard QR took 0.90 to 0.98 on the JIT with AVX2 and 0.95 to 1.01 elsewhere. Over each symbol's quiet-zone-free span row, Micro QR's quiet zone went from 1.18 to 1.26 to 1.06 to 1.11 on the compiled builds (without AVX2 in runs of Micro QR alone, since runs of every shape gained less there, as the review entry says) and from 1.10 to 1.11 to 1.03 to 1.11 interpreted, and Standard QR's class API from 1.07 to 1.11 to 0.99 to 1.07 on the JIT with AVX2. The quiet-zone-free rows read 0.93 to 1.06: Micro QR's run changed code (no clear of the destination, the strided placer's entry), and the others moved within their run's spread. The tables are in the references file ("Phase 8: output edges").

Done.
- `QRCodeData.SetCoreData` packs through `ModuleBitPacker.Pack`, the vector packer of the other two data models, which writes the same stream. The pack took 0.23 to 0.37 of its time on the JIT with AVX2. `QRCodeDataCoreDataParityTest` holds it to an MSB-first pack written from the definition at every version, over a payload that was all dark before.
- `QRCodeData` built from the winner's packed rows was not done. After the packer the pack is 1.6 to 2.5 % of the quiet-zone-free encode, the most this could save, and every scorer tier would have to hand out its winner's rows, column c at bit c in one to three words or as transposed planes, to be reordered into the data model's stream anyway.
- `QuietZoneWindow` holds the quiet zone of the three span outputs. Standard QR's placement pipeline writes a contiguous core, so the core is built at the destination's start and `CenterCore` moves its rows into the window, the last first, clearing each gap between two rows as the row after it moves. The rented buffer and the clear of the whole destination are gone.
- Micro QR writes the window directly, as rMQR does. The placer has a strided overload, every tier taking the row pitch, the BMI2 tier's 32-module store bounded by the last row's end, and the margins are cleared before it: the vector unpack runs past a row only with the row's packed bits past the core, which are zero, so they stay light. The class path's clears of a stack buffer that `stackalloc` already zeroes are gone. Moving the core in place, as Standard QR does, was measured first and left 28 to 41 ns of moves and margins on M1 to M4 where the strided placer leaves 11 to 14 ns of margins (kernel).
- rMQR's two loops of margin clears are `QuietZoneWindow.ClearMargins`.
- A gap of up to 16 bytes is a `Span.Clear` of a constant 8 or 16 bytes ending where the gap ends, which the JIT writes as one store and which also zeroes up to 6 bytes of the row in front, written after it (on builds before .NET 10, 8-byte stores since the review below). As first written, the rows moved and then one `Span.Clear` of the 2q bytes a gap, a call, cleared each gap. That made the in-place move slower than the old clear and copy, by 1.12 to 1.25 at M1 to version 1 in the phase's kernel run, which timed an old form neither symbology had, and by 1.30 to 1.44 from M1 to version 6 against each symbology's own path in pinned runs of the review. The calls were most of it: made as each row moved, they still left the in-place move at 1.07 to 1.20 in the phase's run and 1.21 to 1.32 in the review's. The first A/B read the quiet-zone encodes of Micro QR at 1.09 to 1.10 and of version 1 at 1.03.
- Two costs of moving code were found by the per-build runs and removed with `AggressiveInlining`: the gap clear as a call a row on the WebAssembly interpreter (in one run, the quiet-zone encodes of Micro QR M2 to M4, of three rMQR sizes and of Standard QR at versions 1 and 6 took 1.03 to 1.15 of base there and 1.04 to 1.19 of the build with it inlined), and the Micro QR placer's entry, which the JIT stopped inlining into the generator once it took the stride (without AVX2 the quiet-zone-free M2 and M3 encodes took 1.08 and 1.04 times their time with it inlined).
- Left: on default NativeAOT the M4 placer stage reads 1.11 to 1.16 and its quiet-zone-free and class encodes 1.02 to 1.04, with M2 and M3 at 0.92 to 0.95. ILC's unpack loops are the base's instructions, at another offset, and only M4 runs the inner loop twice a row, so this is taken to be code placement.
- Tests: the dirty-destination tests of all three symbologies run quiet zones on both sides of each gap form's bounds (q = 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 and 9, beside 0 and the defaults, and 25 for Standard QR and Micro QR), Micro QR's with three fills and the tail checked, and the Optimal span tests of Standard QR and Micro QR run on a dirty buffer. `MicroQRModulePlacerParityTest` runs every tier on a dirty matrix, and strided with rows 1, 2, 4 and 50 bytes apart past the core: every core module against the reference, nothing but light modules between rows, nothing past the last row, and the stride and length checks. Of 24 planted faults (the gap forms' bounds, offsets and order, the top and bottom margins, both row loops, each tier's stride, the BMI2 bound, the argument checks, a dark module written past a row, the order of the margins and the placer in both Micro QR paths and in rMQR, the stride the generator passes), all failed a test: the 12 in `QuietZoneWindow` on its form at the commit, the other 12 on the tree before the placer's `AggressiveInlining`, at lines that did not change after. On a machine with the BMI2 tier, Micro QR's tests alone miss the four faults in the gap clear's bounds and offsets, since its 32-module store writes zeros over the bytes they leave. The Standard QR and rMQR tests catch them. The review ran the faults again on the reviewed code (below).
- The corpus hashes are unchanged under AVX2, with AVX off and with hardware intrinsics off: the 7,647 symbols, the 6,504 pinned-mask symbols, the 980 mixed and Structured Append encodes, and a new pass of 3,168 span and class encodes of the three symbologies at quiet zones 0 to 5, 7 to 9, 16 and 25 under both segmentations into one dirty destination. The test suite passes (37,089 tests with 800 skipped, 1,374 skipped with AVX off and 2,305 with hardware intrinsics off), and the timing mode's parity check matches on the JIT with and without AVX2, default NativeAOT, and WebAssembly AOT and interpreted.
- The specs follow: `standardqr-encoder.md` (the span output, two performance lessons), the Micro QR spec map (the output row and its tests), `qrcode-symbologies.md` (`ModuleBitPacker` and `QuietZoneWindow` among the shared components, three lessons).

Lessons.
- The plan's premise about rMQR was wrong. It wrote into the strided window and cleared only the margins, and its quiet zone still cost it 1.12 to 1.20 of the quiet-zone-free encode, about what Micro QR's clear of everything cost. The per-row clear calls were part of that, and with one store a gap it still costs 1.07 to 1.18 on the JIT with AVX2, so the strided form is not free either. A form that looks cheaper is measured before it is copied.
- A clear of a variable few bytes is a call and of a constant few bytes a store. The same `Span.Clear`, given its length as a constant, took the margins to 0.87 to 0.99 of explicit stores' time on the JIT. On .NET 8 the constant form is a store only in a block its profile saw run (review entry below).
- A refactor can cost a build what no kernel benchmark shows. Sharing the gap clear added a call a row on the interpreter, and the Micro QR placer's entry lost the JIT's inline when it took the stride. Each showed only in that build's end-to-end rows, each cost 4 to 19 % against the same build with the attribute in the run that compared them (1 to 15 % against base), and each went with one attribute.
- What a kernel writes past its work decides its contract. Micro QR's unpack overran a row with zeros all along. Written down and tested, that let the margins be cleared first and the placer write the window, and stores that zero exactly the gap, which an overrun of module values would have needed, were 3 to 5 ns slower on the margins of M1 to M4.
- A process that encodes every symbology can read what one encoding a single symbology does not. Without AVX2, the build at this commit read Micro QR's quiet-zone-free and class rows at M3 and M4 1.03 to 1.07 in both runs of every shape, against 0.97 to 1.00 in two runs of Micro QR alone, and in the first of those mixed runs its quiet zone over its quiet-zone-free row stayed at 1.15 to 1.21 (base 1.19 to 1.22). It was not one run's noise, and the cause was not found (review entry below).

### From review of phase 8 (2026-10-06)

An adversarial review in twenty-one rounds found no wrong output for valid input. The first round reviewed the commit and each later one the change as it then stood, and each claim was put to three verifiers. The claims that two verifiers refuted were dropped, and the rest were fixed in this record, the references file, the specs, the code and its comments, the tests and `tools/mutation_check.cs`. The exit, amended on `main` the same day to name the BenchmarkDotNet classes, is now measured on them.

Done.
- .NET 8 compiles a `Span.Clear` of a constant few bytes as a store only in a block its profile saw run, and leaves the other gap form a call for the life of the process. A process that encoded with quiet zones of one form and then of the other paid a call a row. Micro QR M2 at quiet zones 2 and 4 read 171 to 177 ns after a warm-up at 6, against 164 to 172 for base and 140 to 150 after a warm-up at 2 and 4. At quiet zone 6 after a warm-up at 2 and 4 it read 166, base's 164 to 171, against 139 to 142 after a warm-up at 6 (the fastest iteration of each of three runs). Builds before .NET 10 now write the gaps as 8-byte stores, which .NET 8 inlines in either block, and the two cases read 145 to 150 ns and 149 to 167. .NET 10 writes both constant forms as stores whatever its profile saw and keeps the clear.
- On netstandard Standard QR's quiet-zone span keeps the path before the phase, a pooled core copied into the cleared destination. On .NET Framework 4.8 the move in place took 1.13 to 1.14 times that path's time at versions 1 to 20 with one store a gap (quiet zone 4), 1.15 to 1.26 with two (quiet zone 6) and 1.17 to 1.29 with a clear a gap, and 0.99 to 1.09 at version 40 (a kernel, one process). The commit's encode at quiet zone 4 read 4.90 to 4.93 µs at version 1 and 21.3 at version 10, against base 4.78 to 4.80 and 19.9 to 20.0 in the same runs. With the old path it reads 4.78 to 4.86 and 20.4 to 20.6, against base 4.78 to 4.82 and 19.8 to 20.4 in later ones. A build of the commit with base's `QRCodeGenerator.cs` read even with base at version 10 in another alternation (19.97 to 20.10 µs, base 20.02 to 20.05, the commit 21.37 to 21.78), so the commit's excess came with the move, though the kernel puts the move's own work 0.18 µs over the old path there. The shipped old path is base's loop moved into a helper, and its 1.03 of base at version 10 has no measured cause. Micro QR's and rMQR's quiet-zone span paths, which the netstandard builds take rewritten, read 0.74 to 0.81 and 0.97 to 1.01 of base there in two runs of the review (references). netstandard2.1 took the move in place once .NET 6 and 7 were timed (the follow-up below).
- `QRCodeData` packs through `ModuleBitPacker.PackZeroOrOne`: the vector packer where it has a vector step, and otherwise the multiply-gather the model had, since the packer's scalar loop folds every byte to 0 or 1 first and took 1.4 to 1.6 times as long on .NET Framework 4.8 (about twice with intrinsics off on .NET 8). The class encode there read 20.6 to 20.9 µs at version 10 at the commit, against base 20.4 to 20.6. With the gather back it read 19.7 µs at version 10 and 1.00, 1.01 and 0.99 of base at versions 1, 23 and 39. The gather is base's loop, so the gain at version 10 is not the pack's. No test pins `QRCodeData`'s call to `PackZeroOrOne`: on every test leg the entry takes `Pack`, so a return to `Pack` would pass and cost only the netstandard and no-vector processes.
