- `MicroQRModulePlacer.ValidateArguments` is not inlined. Through the `AggressiveInlining` entry its interpolated messages went into the generator's span `CreateCore` on .NET 10 with AVX2, 5.4 KB of code against 3.4 KB with it a call, its prolog zeroing 584 bytes a call against 344.
- `QuietZoneWindow` asserts that its target is exactly the matrix, since both methods clear to its end.
- The rMQR Optimal span path's margin clear had no test on a dirty destination: removing it passed the suite. `RmQRSegmentationTest.Optimal_SpanOverload_MatchesTheDataOverload` now fills the destination, adds a tail, and runs quiet zones 0 to 5, 8 and 9. The removal fails it. `ModuleBitPackerParityTest` holds `PackZeroOrOne` and its scalar route to the naive pack. The strided placer test's comment said the overrun lands in the gaps or the next row, where the BMI2 tier's 32-module store reaches the row after it at sizes 11 and 13, and `QRCodeDataCoreDataParityTest`'s summary now names its pack test.
- Standard QR's quiet-zone span path on netstandard, code of its own since the first round, ran in no test: the test project targets .NET 8 and 10, and nothing else runs a netstandard build. `NetStandardBuildParityTest` loads the netstandard2.0 and 2.1 builds beside the core project, as the dependency tests find them, into a load context of its own, and holds the span outputs of the three symbologies, Single and Optimal, on a dirty destination to the host's build. It asserts that a text of each symbology segments under Optimal into a smaller symbol, so that the planned path runs. Removing the clear at either of Standard QR's span sites fails it.
- `PackZeroOrOne`'s routes pack 0/1 modules alike, so no test told which one ran. `PackZeroOrOne_TakesPack_WhereTheTierTableGivesThePackerAVectorStep` tells them apart with a byte of 0xFF, against the packer's row of the tier table, and fails with the dispatch fixed to the gather. The entry's summary says what any other byte may do, and the test class's summary names Standard QR's entry.
- The phase's kernel timed its quiet-zone forms against an old form that zeroed a 1,024-byte stack buffer, or above 1,024 modules allocated an array, which neither symbology's path did. Against each symbology's own path, in two pinned runs of the review, the move in place as first written took 1.30 to 1.44 from M1 to version 6, and 1.21 to 1.32 there with each gap's clear made as the row after it moved. With the gap stores it took 0.95 to 1.04 there, 0.91 at version 19 and 0.73 at version 40. The phase's run had put the first form at 1.12 to 1.25 and the stores at 0.76 to 0.88 from M1 to version 1, and the stores at 0.48, 0.33 and 0.37 at versions 6, 19 and 40. Part of that difference is between runs: the review's runs read the stores at 0.87 to 0.94 of the phase's old form to version 1 and 0.51 to 0.71 from version 6, and the phase's run was not pinned. The references and the lesson in `qrcode-symbologies.md` give the review's figures.
- The BenchmarkDotNet classes on .NET 10 (ShortRun, two alternating rounds a side, two disturbed base processes left out, and for Micro QR also 15 iterations): Standard QR's class rows took 0.88 to 0.99 of their time and its quiet-zone rows 0.95 to 1.02, Micro QR's quiet-zone rows 0.87 to 0.91 and its class rows 0.98 to 1.02, rMQR's rows 0.94 to 1.02, and the quiet-zone-free rows 0.98 to 1.03 (an rMQR one 1.07). Over each shape's quiet-zone-free row, Standard QR's class rows went from 1.07 to 1.16 to 1.00 to 1.09 and Micro QR's quiet zone from 1.22 to 1.25 to 1.07 to 1.12.
- Without AVX2, two runs of every shape read Micro QR's quiet-zone-free and class rows at M3 and M4 1.03 to 1.07 on the build at the commit. The reviewed build reads those rows at M2 to M4 0.98 to 1.01 in the second run and its quiet zone 0.86 to 0.91 against base, with a base round left out that ran 1.7 to 2.1 times as long on every shape. The run was .NET 10, where both builds' Tier1 span `CreateCore` without AVX2 is the same 3,140 bytes with `ValidateArguments` a call. Their Micro QR code differs in that attribute and in the packer's tail, moved into a method of its own, so the cause is open.
- 30 faults planted in the reviewed code all fail a test: 25 on .NET 10 (the gap forms and margins, the placer's strides, bound and checks, the generators' order and stride, the 0/1 gather) and 5 on .NET 8 (the store forms). On this machine, which takes the BMI2 tier, Micro QR's tests alone catch one of the ten faults in the gap clear's bounds and offsets, a .NET 8 store offset, as the 32-module store writes zeros over the bytes the others leave. A second-round verifier ran the five .NET 10 ones through a copy of Micro QR's dirty-destination test on the other tiers: with the 16-module tier (AVX2 off) it caught the two bounds faults, and with the scalar tier (hardware intrinsics off), which the netstandard builds take, all five. The .NET 8 ones were not run on the other tiers. The corpus hashes are unchanged under AVX2, with AVX off and with hardware intrinsics off, the netstandard builds' span outputs match the host build's on dirty buffers for all three symbologies (`NetStandardBuildParityTest`), and the test suite passes (37,287 tests with 792 skipped, 1,366 skipped with AVX off and 2,297 with hardware intrinsics off, with the netstandard builds current).
- The lessons in `qrcode-symbologies.md` say what the kernel timed and what the window saved, and two are added on .NET 8's constant clear and on .NET Framework 4.8. `standardqr-encoder.md` and the shared-component table name the netstandard path and the 0/1 pack, and `tools/mutation_check.cs` says what it does not measure.
- Not measured: ARM64. The phase moves Standard QR's class pack onto `ModuleBitPacker`'s AdvSimd step and gives the NEON unpack a stride, and no ARM64 machine was at hand. Its tests run on CI's ARM64 legs. Nor were the runtimes that load the netstandard2.1 build, such as .NET 6 and 7 and Mono. .NET Framework 4.8 runs the netstandard2.0 build, and netstandard2.1 shares its code: it keeps Standard QR's old path, and takes Micro QR's and rMQR's rewritten paths, timed only through netstandard2.0. Standard QR's path was timed on .NET 6 and 7 later, and netstandard2.1 now moves the core in place (the follow-up below).

Lessons.
- A build the phase did not measure can lose what the others gained. The move in place was even or faster on .NET 8 and later (even end to end on the JIT, 0.87 to 0.96 on WebAssembly AOT) and slower on .NET Framework 4.8, and the vector packer's scalar fallback, written for any non-zero byte, cost the 0/1 matrix it was given. A change that rewrites a path is measured on netstandard too, or kept from it.
- A constant clear is a store only where the compiler expands it. .NET 8 expands it in a block its profile saw run, so of two constant forms behind a branch one stays a call, and which one depends on what the process did first. An inlined store does not.
- Code compiled only into a build no test host runs is untested, however much of the same path the suite covers. Keeping netstandard's old path split one tested path in two, and only a test that loads the netstandard build beside the core project ran the new half.
- A comment's reason has to come from the caller it describes. The clear's cost on .NET Framework 4.8 was measured in the move in place, and the comment gave it as the reason for the stores in the margin clear, the only caller netstandard keeps. There a verifier's run put the stores at 1.11 and 1.13 of the clear's mean time at quiet zones 4 and 6 (1.02 and 1.05 of its median), so the clear was no slower.
- A kernel's baseline is the old code as it was, not a stand-in for it. The phase's old form zeroed a 1,024-byte buffer, or allocated one, where the paths it stood for zeroed a smaller one or rented, and it showed the move in place winning on the small symbols, where against those paths it was about even. The review's first rerun repeated it with a Micro QR baseline whose clear the JIT expanded at a constant length, where the old code cleared at a length known only at run time, so a baseline is checked line for line against the old commit.

### Phase 8 follow-up, netstandard2.1 on .NET 6 and 7 (2026-10-07)

The review kept Standard QR's old quiet-zone path on netstandard2.1 without timing a runtime that loads that build. .NET 6 and 7 load it, the package having no asset of their own, and .NET 6.0.36 and 7.0.20 were installed for the run. Against `main` (5b666aa), with a harness of its own on the two netstandard2.1 builds (six alternating rounds per runtime, each process pinned to one CCD with the .NET build servers shut down, each row the median of nine rounds of the fastest of fifteen batches, the median of the process medians), the span encode at quiet zone 4 took 0.99 to 1.00 of its time on .NET 6 and 0.98 to 0.99 on .NET 7, where the quiet-zone-free rows the change does not touch read 0.995 to 1.005 and 0.985 to 0.993. Over each symbol's quiet-zone-free row, at quiet zones 4 and 6, the quiet zone went from 0.5 to 2.6 % of a version 1 to 40 encode to 0.3 to 2.1 %, and no symbol's went up on either runtime. The tables are in the references file ("Phase 8", netstandard2.1 on .NET 6 and 7).

Done.
- Standard QR's two quiet-zone span sites move the core in place on netstandard2.1 as on .NET 8 and later (`NETSTANDARD2_1_OR_GREATER || NET5_0_OR_GREATER`, the library's spelling for that set), and `CopyIntoWindow` is compiled for netstandard2.0 alone.
- The kernel, the netstandard2.1 build's own `QuietZoneWindow.CenterCore` against the old path line for line, neither writing the core (three processes per runtime), put the move at 0.72 to 0.99 of the old path's time with one store a gap (quiet zone 4) on .NET 6 and 0.71 to 0.89 on .NET 7. With two (quiet zone 6) it took 0.78 to 0.95 on .NET 7, and on .NET 6 1.07 to 1.09 at versions 1 and 10, 0.99 to 1.01 at version 20 and 0.82 to 0.84 at 40, which the encodes did not show: there the quiet zone at 6 went from 2.14 to 2.07 % at version 1 and from 1.60 to 1.34 % at version 10. With a clear a gap (quiet zone 9) it took 1.36 to 1.48 to version 20 on .NET 6 and 1.14 to 1.27 on .NET 7, and the same build on .NET 8 1.42 to 1.58, a gap over 16 bytes being a call on every build. End to end at quiet zone 9 the quiet zone went from 1.6 to 2.1 % at version 10 on .NET 6 and to 2.0 % on .NET 7, and at version 1 from 2.2 to 2.9 % on .NET 6 and from 2.9 to 2.6 % on .NET 7.
- `NetStandardBuildParityTest.StandardQRQuietZone_KeepsTheOldPathOnNetStandard20Only` tells the two paths apart by the old path's helper, compiled only into a build that keeps the path, and failed on the netstandard2.1 build before the change. The span parity test now runs netstandard2.1's move on a dirty destination at quiet zones that reach each gap form: with the first of the two pre-.NET 10 gap stores removed, its Standard QR case for netstandard2.1 failed on both hosts, where before the change that build took the old path. On the .NET 8 host netstandard2.0's Standard QR case failed too, since the host's own output takes the same stores.
- Both builds wrote the same symbols in every process (16 symbol and quiet-zone outputs, hashed after an encode into a dirty destination). The test suite passes (37,291 tests, 792 skipped) with the netstandard builds current.
- The specs follow: `standardqr-encoder.md` (the span output, the performance lesson) and `qrcode-symbologies.md` (the shared-component row, a lesson). `CopyIntoWindow`'s and `QuietZoneWindow`'s summaries say which builds take which path.
- Left out: a .NET 7 process of the change whose two version 40 rows, the quiet-zone-free one included, read 446 to 452 µs in all nine rounds, 2.7 times the other processes, while its other rows matched theirs.
- Not measured: Mono and .NET Core 3.1, which load netstandard2.1 too, since neither was at hand, and Micro QR's and rMQR's quiet-zone paths on .NET 6 and 7, which this change does not touch.

Lessons.
- A build-wide offset is read off the rows a change cannot reach. On .NET 7 the change's build read 0.985 to 0.993 of base on every quiet-zone-free row, so its quiet-zone rows' 0.98 to 0.99 mixed that offset with the change, and the quiet zone was read over each process's own quiet-zone-free row.
- The decision is read from the encodes, and the kernel explains them only where they agree. On .NET 6 the kernel put the two-store move 6 and 15 ns over the clear and copy at versions 1 and 10, and the encodes' quiet zone still cost less with it. What the kernel leaves out, the core's writes into the rented buffer or into the destination, was not timed apart.
- A runtime past its support is still at hand. `dotnet-install` put .NET 6 and 7 in a folder of their own without touching the machine's install, and a harness built for net6.0 and net7.0 runs the netstandard2.1 build on them, so "not timed" there was a choice.

### Phase 8 follow-up, gaps over 16 bytes (2026-10-07)

From quiet zone 9 a gap between two core rows is more than 16 bytes, and `ClearGap` cleared it with a `Span.Clear` of its length, a call a row, which only kernels on .NET Framework 4.8 and on the netstandard2.1 build had timed. Against `main` (d32274b), with a harness of its own on the net8.0 and net10.0 builds (each process pinned to one CCD with the .NET build servers shut down, each row the median of nine rounds of the fastest of fifteen batches, the median of the process medians), 16-byte stores back from the gap's end, the last at its start, took the span encodes at quiet zones 9, 12 and 16 to 0.88 to 0.91 of their time for Micro QR, 0.95 to 0.99 for Standard QR and 0.96 to 0.99 for rMQR on .NET 8.0.28, and to 0.94 to 0.96, 0.96 to 0.99 and 0.96 to 0.98 on .NET 10.0.9 (six alternating rounds). The rows the change does not reach (quiet zones 0, the default and 8) read 0.97 to 1.03. Over each symbol's quiet-zone-free row, Micro QR's quiet zone there went from 29.9 to 38.7 % to 14.3 to 23.0 % on .NET 8 and from 23.2 to 28.7 % to 15.6 to 25.0 % on .NET 10. On default NativeAOT Micro QR's encodes there took 0.92 to 0.98 on .NET 8 and 0.95 to 0.98 on .NET 10. The WebAssembly interpreter took longer with the stores, so the browser keeps the clear. The tables are in the references file ("Phase 8", gaps over 16 bytes).

Done.
- `ClearGap` writes a gap over 16 bytes as 16-byte stores back from its end, the last at its start: two up to quiet zone 16, three up to 24. Nothing in front of the gap is zeroed. On .NET 10 a store is a constant 16-byte `Span.Clear` and on .NET 8 `Vector128<byte>.Zero.CopyTo`, which .NET 8 inlines in a block its profile did not see run: warmed at quiet zone 8 alone, the wide gap's block held its two stores on both runtimes. The store sits in `QuietZoneWindow.Vector128.cs`, since `SimdLayoutTest` refuses a vector type in the stem file. The netstandard builds and the browser keep the clear. Since the review below, the stores cover gaps of 17 to 32 bytes only, wider gaps keep the clear, and the store is `Vector128<byte>.Zero.CopyTo` on .NET 10 too.
- The kernel, the library's `CenterCore` and `ClearMargins` against copies of them with each gap form, three processes a runtime at quiet zones 8 to 16 on Standard QR's, Micro QR's and rMQR's sizes. The shipped form took 0.45 to 0.83 of the clear's time on .NET 8 and 0.69 to 0.91 on .NET 10, and was slower in no process. 16-byte stores back from the end with up to 14 bytes in front zeroed took 0.47 to 0.81 and 0.76 to 0.96. 8-byte stores took 0.62 to 1.00 and 0.92 to 1.19, slower than the clear on .NET 10 in some process at 50 of the 64 shapes and quiet zones.
- End to end, the A/B above, and for V19 and V40, whose rows moved within 0.02 of their own quiet-zone-free rows, eight more rounds of them alone: their quiet zone over the quiet-zone-free row went from 3.2 to 5.5 % to 2.2 to 4.1 % on .NET 8 and from 3.5 to 5.6 % to 3.0 to 4.7 % on .NET 10.
- WebAssembly, the WebAssembly report from copies of `main` with quiet-zone rows added to its timing mode, under Node. With the stores, quiet zones 9 and 16 took 1.01 to 1.05 of base's time interpreted and 0.90 to 0.98 AOT-compiled. Elsewhere the library gates both WebAssembly builds with one flag, and the interpreter is the default a Blazor WebAssembly app runs, so `OperatingSystem.IsBrowser()` keeps the clear there. With that test both builds read level with base: 0.99 to 1.02 interpreted, 1.00 to 1.03 AOT-compiled.
- Default NativeAOT, the same harness: on .NET 8 Micro QR's rows the change reaches took 0.92 to 0.98, rMQR's 0.94 to 1.00 and Standard QR's 0.98 to 1.00, against 0.96 to 1.01 for the rows it does not reach. On .NET 10 Micro QR's took 0.95 to 0.98 and Standard QR's 1.00 to 1.01. Every quiet-zone row of rMQR R17x139 read 1.04 to 1.06 there, those the change does not reach included, and its quiet-zone-free row 0.96. The two images differ only in `CenterCore` and `ClearMargins`, and every method after them moved, so this is taken to be code placement and left, as for the M4 placer in phase 8.
- Tests: Standard QR's and Micro QR's dirty-destination tests, rMQR's two quiet-zone span tests and the netstandard parity test run quiet zones 16 and 17, the widest gap with two stores and the narrowest with three. In the parity test the host's build writes the stores and the netstandard builds the clear. Of 8 faults planted in the new form (the last store left out or a byte late, the loop's step at 32, its bound at 32 bytes or at the start plus 16, each runtime's store a byte late, the browser test inverted), each of the first seven fails three or four of those test methods on the runtime that compiles it. The inverted test writes the same bytes and fails nothing.
- Every process of both builds wrote the same 72 outputs, on the JIT and on NativeAOT, hashed after an encode into a destination of 0xA5. The test suite passes (37,327 tests, 792 skipped) with the netstandard builds current.
- The specs follow: `qrcode-symbologies.md` (a lesson), `standardqr-encoder.md` (the performance lesson on the move).
- Not measured: ARM64; Mono outside the browser (Android, iOS) and WASI, which take the stores; the netstandard builds with the stores.

Lessons.
- A form that wins on every compiled build can lose on the interpreter. The stores took the place of one clear of a variable length with two of a constant 16 bytes, and from the same source AOT-compiled WebAssembly gained 2 to 10 % at quiet zones 9 and 16 where the interpreter lost 1 to 5 %. Why was not measured, so the interpreter is timed whenever a change rewrites a per-row path, whatever the other builds show.
- A store loop is not cheaper than a call at every length. 8-byte stores back from the gap's end beat the clear on .NET 8 at 63 of the kernel's 64 shapes and quiet zones and lost to it on .NET 10 at 50. Two 16-byte stores beat it on both.
- A layout shift can move rows the change does not run. On .NET 10 NativeAOT the change grew two methods, and rMQR R17x139's rows at the default quiet zone and at 8, which run none of the new code, read 1.05 to 1.06 while its quiet-zone-free row read 0.96. A row the change cannot reach is read beside every row it can, per symbol.

### From review of the gap stores (2026-10-08)

An adversarial review of the follow-up, each claim put to three verifiers, found no wrong output and confirmed three claims, all on speed. The store loop had no upper bound and lost to the clear on wide gaps. On 32-bit x86 under .NET 10 the constant 16-byte clear was a call, so the stores cost two calls a row. And no test could tell which form a row took. Against `main` (d32274b), with the follow-up's harness (alternating rounds, each process pinned to one CCD with the .NET build servers shut down), the reviewed code took Micro QR's span encodes at quiet zones 9 and 16 to 0.88 to 0.89 of their time on the .NET 8 JIT and 0.91 to 0.94 on .NET 10 (x64), 0.92 to 0.98 on 32-bit x86 and 0.92 to 0.99 on default NativeAOT. From quiet zone 17 up, where both builds clear the gap, Micro QR's and rMQR's encodes read 0.96 to 1.03 on every build but for one rMQR row on x86 .NET 10 (R11x59 at 64, 1.08). The tables are in the references file ("Phase 8", gaps over 16 bytes, from the review).

Done.
- `ClearGap` writes two 16-byte stores for a gap of 17 to 32 bytes only (quiet zones 9 to 16), one ending where the gap ends and one starting where it starts, and clears a wider gap as before. In this record's kernel the committed loop won at quiet zone 32 (0.73 to 1.00 of the clear's time on x64) and took 1.01 to 1.43 at 64 and 128. The fix takes 1.00 to 1.07 on x64 at 128.
- `Clear16` is `Vector128<byte>.Zero.CopyTo` on .NET 10 too. 32-bit x86 on .NET 10 compiled the constant `Span.Clear` of 16 as a call to `SpanHelpers.ClearWithoutReferences`, so the committed form made two calls a row where the clear made one. Its kernel took 1.22 to 2.89 of the clear's time at quiet zones 9 to 128, and the review's end-to-end runs read 1.01 to 1.06 at 9 and 16. The vector store is one instruction there, and the fix's kernel takes 0.77 to 0.98 at 9 and 16 (the median of two processes), but for M4 at quiet zone 9, where one process read 1.95 and the other 0.76.
- No test tells the forms apart: deleting the `return;` that ended the store block, inverting the browser test or narrowing the bound to 30 bytes passes the suite on both hosts, since every form writes the same bytes. The stage harness has `e2e-qz8`, `-qz9`, `-qz16` and `-qz17` rows for each Standard QR, Micro QR and rMQR stage symbol, on both sides of each form's bound, so a build's form can be timed on the JIT, NativeAOT and WebAssembly.
- Of 7 faults planted in the new form, the five that change bytes (either store left out, the start store a byte late, the bound at 34 bytes, the vector store a byte late) each fail three or four test methods on net8.0 and net10.0. The bound at 30 bytes and the inverted browser test write the same bytes and fail none.
- On x64 and x86, .NET 8 and .NET 10, the two-store block is two `vmovups` and the wider gap's block one call.
- .NET 8 compiles the clear in a block its profile did not see run as a call to `SpanHelpers.ClearWithoutReferences`. Before, every gap over 16 bytes took one block; now quiet zones 9 to 16 and 17 up take two. So in a process whose profile saw quiet zones 9 to 16 and not wider ones, the wider clear is that call where it had been expanded: the kernel, which times quiet zone 9 first, read 1.10 to 1.27 at quiet zone 17 on .NET 8. A process that starts at the default quiet zone, as the end-to-end runs do, compiles both builds' wider clear as the same call. The kernel also read 1.03 to 1.08 at quiet zone 17 on .NET 10 x64 and 0.96 to 1.12 on x86, where the clear is the same call in both builds; end to end, Micro QR's and rMQR's rows there read 0.97 to 1.03.
- Every process of both builds wrote the same 108 outputs, on the JIT (x64 and x86) and on NativeAOT. The test suite passes (37,327 tests, 792 skipped) with the netstandard builds current.
- The specs follow: `qrcode-symbologies.md` (the lesson on the stores, the scope of the constant clear's lesson), `standardqr-encoder.md` (the performance lesson on the move).
- Not measured: WebAssembly with the reviewed code, where the browser test comes before the gap's size and takes the clear as the code it replaces did; ARM64; Mono outside the browser and WASI.

Lessons.
- A form measured where it wins is bounded where it was measured. The loop was timed at quiet zones 9, 12 and 16 and ran unbounded to 10,000, and on x64 a loop of 16-byte stores lost to the clear between quiet zones 32 and 64.
- A constant clear is a store only where the compiler expands it, and that is not every target of one runtime: .NET 10 on 32-bit x86 calls for 8 or 16 bytes where x64 stores, so the gap stores are vector stores.
- A new branch in front of an old form splits its profile. On .NET 8 the clear is expanded only in a block the profile saw run, so the form a process ran first decides whether the other is a call.
